problem: Object-goal inspection methods (coverage planning, SB2G, frontier-based semantic methods) cannot exploit floor-plan priors and commonsense knowledge; they cover unexplored areas until the target is seen, or use myopic frontier selection. LLM planners are too heavy for robots with limited compute and no internet, and they reason poorly about probabilities and space.
motivation: Real-world inspection (urban buildings, construction sites) has large search spaces, and humans use floor plans plus commonsense (fire extinguishers are near kitchens and entrances) to search efficiently. Robots in industrial sites cannot rely on onboard LLMs or remote access, so this knowledge must be distilled into a lightweight model and combined with probabilistic non-myopic planning.
key_idea: Distill LLM commonsense about object-to-room-type occurrence into a small Bayesian relational semantic network, then plan room-level search over a floor-plan scene graph with an MDP that minimizes expected travel distance.
insight: Non-myopic MDP planning with calibrated room probabilities beats both a semantic-utility greedy heuristic and a GPT-4 chain-of-thought planner given the same information. GPT-4 fails at probabilistic and spatial trade-offs, e.g. it goes to the nearest bathroom for clothes instead of the bedroom and bathroom jointly. The appendix shows a limitation: when the object sits in a room the RSN rates below 0.5, SPL drops below that of Room Coverage until Bayesian updates correct the prior. In the multi-run coffee-mug experiment, the Brier score falls and SPL rises as the robot observes mugs.
method: Dynamic Scene Graph: hierarchical graph (location/object, room, building layers) built from floor plans, with uniformly sampled location nodes; updated online with traversability risk and newly detected objects

Relational Semantic Network: BGE-small text embedding, then a 3-hidden-layer MLP predicting P(object in each of 27 Matterport3D room types) and P(found without careful local search), then a naive-Bayes update from the robot's observations
RSN training data: GPT-4 queried for 100 object names and for their per-room-type probabilities (5 objects per query); MLP trained on these with text embeddings so it generalizes to similar objects

Semantic-guided global planner: MDP whose states are rooms and whose actions are move-to-room or search-current-room (|U|=2|V2|); goal-transition probability comes from the RSN and cost is A* distance or coverage distance; solved by value iteration in a receding-horizon loop

Local finite-state controller (SB2G-based): global navigation controller with risk-aware MPC, active semantic search controller when the target is possibly detected, and inspection controller to approach the target within radius epsilon
Open-vocabulary extension: replace the text encoder and MLP with direct LLM queries when an LLM is available

setting.backbone: BGE-small embedding + MLP (trained on GPT-4-distilled labels), Bayesian network, MDP value iteration; YOLO detector on hardware
setting.model_size: BGE-small 33M parameters plus a small MLP
setting.training_data: GPT-4-generated probabilities for 100 object names over 27 room types; no Matterport3D or environment-specific object placement data
setting.observation: floor plan / blueprint prior, LIDAR SLAM map, RGB camera object detections
setting.action_space: room-level global actions (go to room / search room locally) executed by MPC low-level trajectories
setting.simulator: Habitat (Matterport3D), ROS Gazebo (Spot office), real world
setting.privileged: floor plan / hierarchical room layout (Matterport3D room annotations in the Habitat experiments) given as prior; room connectivity assumed static

numbers.eval_set_note: 5 Matterport3D scenes, 10 objects, 50 simulations per method; fixed objects (e.g. bed, sink)
numbers.extra: Uses room-level scene layout as prior; does not remember previous runs

numbers.eval_set_note: 5 Matterport3D scenes, 10 objects, 50 simulations per method; movable objects (e.g. clothes, towel)
numbers.extra: Uses room-level scene layout as prior; does not remember previous runs

numbers_note: Only Table I gives quantitative results. The Gazebo SPL comparison against SB2G (Fig. 5), the Brier/SPL curves over runs (Fig. 6), and the hardware run (SPL=0.93 in text, single run) are figure results or single-trial values. Baselines in Table I: GPT-4 Planner 0.84/0.81, Semantic Utility 0.74/0.70, Room Coverage 0.77/0.65, Random 0.65/0.68 (fixed/movable).
results: On Matterport3D in Habitat, SEEK gets SPL 0.96 on fixed and 0.84 on movable objects, beating the strongest baseline, the GPT-4 planner (0.84 and 0.81). In Gazebo it achieves higher SPL and lower path variance than SB2G geometric coverage. On a Spot robot it reached the nearest fire extinguisher with SPL 0.93.
limitations: Requires a floor plan / room layout and assumes static room connectivity
Room-level planning relies on RSN priors; unexpected object placements degrade SPL below room coverage until the belief updates
Closed vocabulary limited to about 100 training objects and 27 room types; hardware validation is a single office building with a small number of trials
